text.p: British markets gave a cautious welcome to Labour's first budget in 18 years, as Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown tightened fiscal policy more stringently than anticipated.
Analysts said on first reading the measures may take the pressure off for further interest rate increases.
Shares pushed higher while bonds were steady after a brief fillip higher. The pound, however, retreated further from recent five-year highs as the prospect of higher interest rates receded.

"The net fiscal tightening is higher than the consensus," Andrew Snowball, treasury economist at Cooperative Bank in London. "The thing people are looking at now is what the 5.5 billion will be made up of."
Brown said his first budget would exercise a net fiscal tightening on the economy of 5.5 billion pounds ($9.1 billion) this year 4.75 billion next year.
Economists had expected a net tightening of around 4.0 billion pounds for 1997.
The FTSE-100 share index was quoted at 4761.5 at 1521 GMT, up 32.8 points or 0.69 percent on the day and compared with 4731.5 before the budget.
September gilt futures on LIFFE were quoted at 114-25, up 5/32 on the day but off the contract high of 115-05 set earlier.

The pound fell more than one pfennig against the mark from pre-budget levels but rebounded more than half that later. It was quoted at 2.8980/90 compared with 2.9025/35 and an initial low at 2.8870. ($ = 0.602 British Pounds)
